title: Status Bits
body:
The **indirect** result of an instruction. You do not ask for them, you get them: almost
every arithmetic, logic, and move instruction sets them as a side effect, and the next
instruction can branch on what they say. They live in the user half of the
[[Status Register]], the low byte, sometimes called the condition code register.

Five bits on the 68000:

| Bit | Name | Set when |
|---|---|---|
| `X` | Extend | copy of C, kept for multi-precision arithmetic |
| `N` | Negative | the result's most significant bit is 1 |
| `Z` | Zero | the result is all zeros |
| `V` | Overflow | the *signed* result does not fit |
| `C` | Carry | a carry or borrow out of the most significant bit |

## Carry versus overflow

The one exam distinction. They answer different questions about the same addition:

- **C** is for [[Integer Representation|unsigned]]: the true result needed one more bit.
- **V** is for signed: the sign came out wrong, adding two positives gave a negative or two
  negatives gave a positive.

```
%0111_1111 + %0000_0001 = %1000_0000
```

As bytes: unsigned that is 127 + 1 = 128, perfectly correct, C stays clear. Signed it is
127 + 1 = −128, badly wrong, so V is set. The hardware sets both flags every time and lets
you choose which one to believe, because it has no idea which interpretation you meant. See
[[Complements]].

## Using them

You rarely read the bits directly. You either compare and branch, or you test and branch:

```
cmp.w   d1,d0        ; computes d0 - d1, keeps only the flags
beq     equal        ; Z set
bne     notequal     ; Z clear
blt     less         ; signed:   N ≠ V
bcs     borrow       ; unsigned: C set
tst.l   d0           ; sets N and Z from d0 alone
```

`cmp` is a `sub` that throws the answer away. That is the whole trick, and it is why
comparison costs nothing extra.

Two traps: pick the signed branch (`blt`, `bge`) or the unsigned one (`bcs`, `bhi`) to match
how you are reading the number, and remember that instructions *between* the compare and the
branch will clobber the flags. `move` sets N and Z too.
